newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Twenty killed in mosque attack in Pakistan.
newsitem.headline: Twenty killed in mosque attack in Pakistan.

text.p: Four gunmen attacked a Sunni Moslem mosque in the central Pakistani city of Multan on Monday, killing 20 people and wounding 56, ambulance sources said.
The attack followed the killing on Sunday night of a leader of the militant Shi'ite Moslem Sipah-i-Mohammad Pakistan (SMP) group in Bahawalpur, about 95 km (60 miles) south of Multan.
Shi'ite sources in Islamabad said Qamar Haider, described as a divisional commander of the SMP, had been shot dead by unidentified gunmen while sitting in his shop.
The mosque attack occurred three days after Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto's estranged brother Murtaza was shot dead in the southern city of Karachi in a shootout between his bodyguards and police.
It was the latest in a bloody feud between religious militants in Pakistan. Shi'ites account for about 15 percent of the country's 130 million people, most of whom are Sunnis.

Witnesses in Multan said three gunmen burst into the Al-Khair Mosque in the mainly Shi'ite-populated Mumtazabad area and opened fire as the congregation was offering dawn prayers. They escaped in a white car driven by a fourth man.
Shahid Ansari, a local councillor, said his father had been in the mosque, frequented by supporters of the militant Sunni Ahl-e-Hadith organisation, but had escaped unhurt.

"He told me that as soon as the worshippers kneeled in prayer, the gunmen opened up with automatic weapons, firing from three sides," he said. "The shooting went on for five minutes and there was blood and bits of flesh all over the mosque."
Ambulances ferried casualties to the city's main Nishtar hospital. Rescue workers listed the names of 20 dead. Hospital doctors said 56 people had been wounded.

Witnesses said the relatives of three of the dead had removed their bodies from the hospital without waiting for a post-mortem and recited funeral prayers outside the mosque, joined by thousands of mourners.
Angry protesters blocked the main Multan-Bahawalpur road with burning barricades after the killings, witnesses said.

Police said the mosque, one of the biggest in the southern district of Mumtazabad, was controlled by the hardline Sunni Sipah-i-Sahaba Pakistan (SSP) group, to which Ahl-e-Hadith is affiliated. A religious school is attached to the mosque.
Sectarian tension has been especially acute in the populous Punjab province, where Multan and Bahawalpur are located.
The SMP's leader, Shi'ite Murid Abbas Yazdani, was shot dead at his home in Islamabad on September 12.
Gunmen killed 12 people in an SSP procession in Karachi on August 14. Up to 18 Shi'ites died four days later in an attack on a community meeting near Mailsi, in Punjab.
